1. A colleague fits a logistic regression and finds one predictor has an OR of 45,000 with an enormous standard error. What is the most likely explanation? Is it an error to fix with a different technique?

Almost certainly separation: the predictor (or a combination of predictors) perfectly or almost perfectly predicts the outcome, so the ordinary maximum likelihood estimate does not exist and the coefficient drifts towards infinity. The data are not wrong, and the 45,000 must not be reported. First look at why the predictor separates the outcome so cleanly (a coding error, a predictor that is really a consequence of the outcome, very small numbers). If the pattern is genuine, valid finite estimates can be obtained with Firth’s penalised likelihood (Heinze & Schemper, 2002) or exact logistic regression.

2. Explain what “linearity in the logit” means, and why checking it on a plot of raw probability against the predictor would be the wrong approach.

The model assumes that each continuous predictor has a straight-line relation with the log-odds of the outcome: logit(p) = b₀ + b₁x. On the probability scale the correctly specified model is S-shaped, so a curved probability plot is expected and says nothing about whether the assumption holds. Check on the logit scale instead: add a quadratic term (or a spline) and see whether the fit improves, or group the predictor and see whether the log-odds of the groups lie roughly on a line.

3. Of 20 children screened, 5 are anaemic. Write the likelihood for the prevalence p, find the MLE, and give its logit. What probability corresponds to a logit of 1.2?

L(p) = p⁵(1 − p)¹⁵. ln L = 5 ln p + 15 ln(1 − p); its slope 5/p − 15/(1 − p) = 0 gives 5(1 − p) = 15p, so p̂ = 5/20 = 0.25. logit(0.25) = ln(0.25/0.75) = ln(1/3) = −1.099. Logit 1.2 → p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−1.2)) = 1 ÷ (1 + 0.301) = 0.77.

1. A logistic regression reports an OR of 1.08 per year of age. A colleague says this means a 30-year age gap corresponds to 30 × 1.08 = 32.4-fold higher odds. What is wrong, and what is the correct figure?

A per-unit OR multiplies once for each unit; it does not add. The coefficient is additive on the log-odds scale (30 × ln 1.08 = 30 × 0.0770 = 2.309), so the OR for 30 years is e^2.309 = 1.08³⁰ = 10.06, about a 10-fold increase in odds, not 32.4.

2. Two logistic models on the same data report the same OR for a predictor, but one discriminates well between cases and non-cases and the other does not. How is this possible?

Discrimination depends on how well all the predictors together separate people who had the event from those who did not, through the spread of the predicted probabilities. A single OR describes one predictor’s association. One model may contain other strong predictors that spread the predicted probabilities widely (good discrimination), while the other contains only weak predictors, so everyone gets a similar predicted probability (poor discrimination), even though the shared predictor’s OR is the same.

3. In a cohort, the 1-year risk of TB is 1% in adults with neither diabetes nor undernutrition, 1.5% with undernutrition only, 2% with diabetes only and 4% with both. Compute the multiplicative interaction ratio and the RERI, and say what each means.

RR₁₀ (undernutrition only) = 1.5/1 = 1.5; RR₀₁ (diabetes only) = 2/1 = 2; RR₁₁ = 4/1 = 4. Multiplicative: RR₁₁ ÷ (RR₁₀ × RR₀₁) = 4 ÷ 3 = 1.33. The joint risk ratio is a third larger than the product of the separate ones: positive interaction on the multiplicative scale. Additive: RERI = 4 − 1.5 − 2 + 1 = 1.5. The excess risks would add to 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 percentage points; the observed joint excess is 3 points. Positive additive interaction: if these associations are causal, correcting undernutrition prevents more TB per person reached among diabetics (4% → 2%, 2 cases per 100) than among non-diabetics (1.5% → 1%, 0.5 per 100).

1. A multinomial model of cause of under-five death uses “other” as the reference. How would the reported results change if “pneumonia” were the reference, and what would stay the same?

Every set of coefficients would now compare a category with pneumonia (diarrhoea vs pneumonia, malnutrition vs pneumonia, other vs pneumonia) instead of with “other”, so all the reported ORs change in value and meaning. The model’s fit, its predicted probabilities for each category, and its likelihood are unchanged: the reference is a reporting choice, and any comparison can be recovered from either parameterisation (e.g. diarrhoea vs pneumonia = (diarrhoea vs other) ÷ (pneumonia vs other)). State the reference.

2. Why is ordinal logistic regression a mistake for an unordered outcome such as blood group?

The ordinal model estimates cumulative odds across cut-points in a fixed order (for example A < B < AB < O) and forces one OR per predictor across all cut-points. Blood groups have no order, so the cut-points, the cumulative odds and the single OR are all artefacts of an arbitrary ordering. A different arbitrary order would give different results. A multinomial model is the right one.

3. In a 1:1 matched case-control study of 100 pairs, 30 pairs have only the case exposed and 12 have only the control exposed. Compute the matched OR and its 95% CI. What would an unconditional logistic model with 99 pair dummies report?

OR = b/c = 30/12 = 2.5. SE(ln OR) = √(1/30 + 1/12) = √0.1167 = 0.342. 95% CI = exp(ln 2.5 ± 1.96 × 0.342) = exp(0.916 ± 0.670) = 1.28 to 4.88. Unconditional logistic regression with a dummy for each pair suffers from sparse data; for 1:1 pairs it gives the square of the conditional OR (Pearce, 2016): 2.5² = 6.25, a serious overestimate.

1. A Poisson regression of malaria cases on “near standing water”, with log(village population) as an offset, gives exp(b) = 2.30. Is this a rate ratio or a count ratio? What would exp(b) be without the offset in these data, and why does it differ?

A rate ratio (incidence rate ratio): with the offset, the model is for log(cases/population). Villages near water have 2.30 times the malaria rate of the others (20.1 vs 8.74 per 1,000). Without the offset, exp(b) is the ratio of mean cases per village, 38.2/23.6 = 1.62. It is smaller because the villages near water have fewer people (9,500 vs 13,500 in total), so their counts understate their rate.

2. A Poisson model shows clear overdispersion. What does switching to negative binomial regression change, and what does it leave unchanged?

It changes the variance assumption from Var = μ to Var = μ + αμ², so the model is fitted against a different likelihood. The coefficient estimates can shift somewhat (IRR 2.30 → 2.47 in the malaria data), and the SEs and CIs widen to reflect the extra variation (1.83–2.89 → 1.70–3.60), making tests more honest. The meaning of exp(b) is unchanged: still a rate ratio with an offset, a count ratio without.

3. A Poisson model of monthly diarrhoea episodes has Pearson χ² = 40 on 10 residual df. Compute the dispersion statistic. If an NB fit gives α = 0.1, what variance does it imply for a child whose expected count is 2 episodes? For an expected count of 20?

Dispersion statistic = 40/10 = 4, well above 1: the counts vary about four times as much as the Poisson model allows (a rough check; confirm with the likelihood-ratio test of α = 0). NB variance = μ + αμ². μ = 2: 2 + 0.1 × 4 = 2.4 (close to Poisson). μ = 20: 20 + 0.1 × 400 = 60, three times the Poisson variance. Overdispersion under the NB model grows with the mean.

1. In a cohort, 40% of unexposed people develop the outcome, and a crude OR is 2.0. Convert it to an RR. What would the RR be if the unexposed risk were 2%?

RR = OR ÷ (1 − p₀ + p₀ × OR). p₀ = 0.40: RR = 2.0 ÷ (1 − 0.40 + 0.80) = 2.0 ÷ 1.40 = 1.43. p₀ = 0.02: RR = 2.0 ÷ (1 − 0.02 + 0.04) = 2.0 ÷ 1.02 = 1.96. With a common outcome the OR of 2 corresponds to a much smaller RR; with a rare outcome the two almost coincide.

2. Why does a Poisson model with a log link give valid prevalence ratios for a 0/1 outcome, and why must its SEs be replaced by robust ones?

The coefficients depend only on the model for the mean, log(p) = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …, which is the prevalence-ratio model; the Poisson likelihood is used only as a working device to estimate it, and it gives consistent estimates when the mean model is right (Zou, 2004). But the Poisson model assumes Var(Y) = p, whereas a 0/1 outcome has Var(Y) = p(1 − p), which is smaller. The model-based SEs are therefore too large (by about 1/√(1 − p); for the CBHI prevalence of 30%, 0.0816 against the correct 0.0683). The robust (sandwich) SE uses the observed residuals instead of the assumed variance and corrects this.

3. A colleague fits a log-binomial model and gets “algorithm did not converge”. Name two alternatives that still give an adjusted prevalence ratio.

  1. Modified Poisson regression: a Poisson model with a robust (sandwich) SE (Zou, 2004). (ii) Marginal standardisation from a logistic model: predict every person’s probability as if exposed and as if unexposed, average each, and take the ratio. (Supplying starting values to the log-binomial model sometimes helps but, as with the CBHI data, may still fail.)
